title: Alkenes and addition reactions
note: Adding HX or water with acid goes through the more stable carbocation (Markovnikov) and can rearrange. Oxymercuration also gives Markovnikov products but never rearranges. Hydroboration puts OH on the less substituted carbon with syn addition. Halogens add anti through a bridged halonium ion.

read.title: Where the hydrogen goes
text: An alkene's π electrons make it a nucleophile, so many reagents add across the double bond. With HBr, the π bond first grabs a proton. The proton goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens, because that leaves the positive charge on the more substituted carbon, where alkyl groups stabilize it. Bromide then adds to that cation. This is Markovnikov's rule, and acid-catalyzed hydration follows it too. Because a free carbocation forms, a hydride or methyl group can shift to make an even more stable cation first.

Other methods give different results. Oxymercuration–demercuration also places OH on the more substituted carbon, but it goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, so no rearrangement occurs. Hydroboration–oxidation reverses the orientation: boron adds to the less hindered carbon and hydrogen to the other in one concerted, syn step, and oxidation then replaces boron with OH. With peroxides, HBr also adds anti-Markovnikov, but by a radical chain.

Bromine adds through a three-membered bromonium ion. Bromide must attack from the opposite face, so the two bromines end up anti. If water is the solvent, water opens the ring at the more substituted carbon and gives a bromohydrin.
